title: Exposure to the Russian Internet Research Agency foreign influence campaign on Twitter in the 2016 US election and its relationship to attitudes and voting behavior
screen_reason: Behavioural study linking a three-wave YouGov panel of 1,496 US Twitter users to their Twitter timelines (1.2 billion posts) and flagging the posts that came from foreign influence campaign accounts on Twitter's own released state-backed account lists. It reports the share of respondents exposed at least once (REACH: 70% to any foreign influence campaign, 63% to Russian accounts), the concentration of exposure across users (1% of users = 70% of exposures; 10% = 98%) and across sources (1% of Russian accounts = 89% of content), and mean per-day exposure intensity. The paper frames the content as 'Russian disinformation'.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Accounts, not claims, were designated: "we use data released by Twitter to identify the posts in survey respondents' timelines that originated from the foreign influence campaigns that were active in the lead-up to the 2016 US election" (Twitter's Election Integrity collection). estimates.moderator_quote: The survey data contain responses from 1496 US respondents who consented both to provide their Twitter account information for research purposes and to answer questions concerning their political attitudes and beliefs at multiple points during the 2016 US election campaign ... To capture the tweets that would appear in respondents' Twitter timelines during the election campaign, we collected the list of users whom respondents followed on Twitter, and retrieved all posts from these users that were sent in the eight months prior to election day ... In aggregate, these tweets constitute 1.2 billion social media posts across all respondents.
estimates.notes: breadth is blank because the classification is a source-level account list (Twitter's state-backed account designations), not a veracity judgement on individual posts. Exposure is POTENTIAL exposure: "although we can observe potential exposures (that is, tweets and retweets by accounts that a given user follows), we cannot know which tweets in their timelines users actually saw." missed_or_uncertain: (1) '86% of all exposures in respondents' timelines in the lead-up to the election among the foreign influence campaigns included herein' were Russian - a within-misinformation composition share (which state campaign), not a prevalence of misinformation in a general denominator; not extracted. (2) Benchmark concentration figures for non-misinformation content ('1% of respondents account for 24% and 37% of exposures to posts from domestic news media and politicians') are not misinformation estimates. (3) '32 million US Twitter users were potentially exposed' is an explicit back-of-the-envelope extrapolation (0.63 x 51 million) using Pew penetration and Census population, and Facebook's 126 million and Twitter's 288 million views are figures the paper cites from company testimony - all excluded by R8. (4) 'Individual respondents were exposed on average to between two and ten posts from foreign influence campaigns per day' is a range over the campaign period (range_not_point) and overlaps the extracted intensity row, so it is not duplicated. (5) 'The share of retweets as an exposure pathway grew steadily over time, reaching 75-80% by election day' is a pathway composition within misinformation exposures, given only as a range and only in a supplementary figure. (6) All attitude, polarization and vote-choice results are effect estimates, not prevalence.

rob.design: Three-wave longitudinal YouGov survey of 1,496 US respondents (wave 1 April 2016; final pre-election wave end of October 2016; post-election recontact on turnout and vote choice) who consented to link their Twitter accounts; sample described as approximately representative of the demographic profile of the US voting-age public and compared to Pew estimates of the Twitter population; no response rate reported. Timelines reconstructed by collecting each respondent's followees and retrieving all their posts in the eight months before election day (1.2 billion posts); posts from foreign influence campaigns identified using account lists released by Twitter (Election Integrity collection), which the authors could not independently validate. Exposure is POTENTIAL exposure (a post appearing in the timeline), not verified viewing. Observational design; NYU IRB 12-9058. Concentration measured by empirical cumulative distributions.
rob.item6_quote: Finally, we use data released by Twitter to identify the posts in survey respondents' timelines that originated from the foreign influence campaigns that were active in the lead-up to the 2016 US election (see Supplementary Methods A1 for more details on Twitter data releases). Following similar studies, we refer to tweets that survey respondents were potentially exposed to in their timelines as their "exposures".
rob.item10_quote: We find that 70% (n = 1042) of respondents were exposed to one or more posts from a foreign influence campaign between April and November 2016, with 786,634 posts from these campaigns identified across all respondents' timelines (n = 1496).
